title: 3 Ways You Should Never Praise Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes genuine praise from false praise, warning that praise given for the teacher's own benefit undermines its power. He identifies three misuses: praising for personal gain to placate a difficult student, praising one student to manipulate the whole group's compliance, and praising out of an obligation to praise constantly regardless of real accomplishment. Each, he argues, is fundamentally about the teacher's needs rather than honest recognition of student achievement. He explains that false praise lowers standards, inflates students' sense of their own abilities, and cheapens genuine accomplishment by treating it the same as baseline compliance. The piece calls for praise that is rare, sincere, and reserved for true, individually-measured accomplishment.
points: Praise given to placate or manage a difficult student's behavior is disingenuous and about the teacher's needs, not the student's achievement.
Publicly praising one student's expected behavior to manipulate the whole class ('caught being good') is a form of manipulation, not honest recognition.
Praising constantly out of a felt obligation dilutes the meaning of praise and blurs the line between compliance and real accomplishment.
False praise lowers standards and gives students an inflated sense of their abilities.
Genuine praise must be reserved for true accomplishment, judged individually and delivered sincerely.
quotes: Too many teachers, though, praise not out of genuineness, not out of a pure motive to highlight hard-earned achievement or excellence . . . But out of their own desires.
The student is praised not in response to any valid improvement, success, or accomplishment, but rather in an effort to mollify, satisfy, appease, and otherwise keep in check for as long as possible.
Often called “caught being good,” this too is disingenuous. The teacher isn’t really impressed with David.
The problem with false praise is that it lowers the standard of what is good. It gives students an inflated sense of their own abilities.
A deeply moving poem, then, chiseled and shaped through hours of dedicated work, gets the same reaction from the teacher as does sitting up straight in one’s chair.
It must be genuine and real and come from the stirrings in your heart.
